04

How TELUS got here

the arc you'd inherit
1990
Alberta Government Telephones privatised

Roots as a provincial Crown telco — origin of the TELUS name and Western Canada stronghold.

1999
BC TELECOM merger

Merges with BC Tel, cementing dominance across BC and Alberta — base of today's fibre footprint.

2000s
National wireless expansion

Builds coast-to-coast mobile, joins the entrenched "Big Three."

2013
Verizon threat evaporates

Verizon rules out entering Canada — no serious foreign competitor has arrived since.

2020
TELUS International (Digital) IPO

The BPO/AI-services arm goes public — diversification beyond connectivity begins in earnest.

2023
5G Standalone network live

Lower latency, network slicing, IoT readiness — the platform for the next B2B revenue layer.

2025
Infra-monetisation & Digital taken private

Sells stakes to deleverage; buys back 100% of TELUS Digital (~US$539M) to own the AI/SaaS engine.

Your advantages & your soft floor

the CEO thesis
Moat

Best-in-class churn

0.91% postpaid churn — lowest of the Big Three. Loyalty and bundling discipline you protect at all costs.

Moat

Diversification beyond pipes

Health, Agriculture, Digital give revenue lines rivals can't copy — margin when telecom is flat.

Moat

Fibre + 5G SA footprint

Deep FTTH in the West plus a live 5G Standalone core = premium internet ARPU and B2B/IoT optionality.

Risk

Mobile ARPU erosion

Competitive pricing drags phone ARPU. Decelerating — but the number the Street watches.

Risk

Saturation ceiling

92% internet, ~88% smartphone. Growth must come from ARPU, adjacencies and share-steal.

Risk

Capital intensity & debt

Spectrum and fibre pushed sector leverage above norms — hence infra stake sales.

◈ The 90-second board pitch: "TELUS wins by being the loyalty leader in a saturated market — I defend the 0.91% churn, accelerate the health/digital/IoT flywheel to escape the ARPU trap, and monetise passive infrastructure to fund the fibre endgame without diluting shareholders. We don't out-scale Rogers; we out-retain and out-diversify them."

The flanker-brand war

each Big Three carrier runs a fighter brand

Below the flagship, each incumbent runs mid-tier and prepaid brands on the same towers — identical coverage, separate service — to absorb price-shoppers without dragging premium ARPU down. This is where Freedom's low-cost 5G is attacked. Fido is Rogers' flanker; Koodo is yours.

This is also why the M&A playbook flags a fighter-brand MVNO play: it's the proven mechanism to fight Quebecor's 20%-cheaper plans without cutting flagship TELUS pricing.

The PureFibre landscape

homes passed · FTTH vs cable

The 5-year price lock — TELUS's exclusive weapon

11

How subscribers interchange across the bundle

stickiness = services per household

The core mechanic: the more services a household holds, the harder it is to leave. A mobile-only customer churns easily; a household with mobile + fibre + security + a parent's fall-detection pendant almost never does. This is why the services war is the churn war.

The pull-through engine

  • →Fibre pulls TV — IP-based TELUS TV rides the PureFibre build
  • →Internet unlocks security — in BC/AB, SmartHome requires TELUS internet
  • →Mobility discounts everything — $10/mo off security, $10 off LivingWell for Mobility customers
  • →Health captures the aging household — the pendant keeps the whole family on TELUS

Why it beats Rogers & Bell

  • ◈Each added service drops churn probability materially
  • ◈TELUS can stack 6 lines on one bill; Rogers/Bell top out at ~4
  • ◈Health + security are contract-based (3–5 yr) — structurally sticky
  • ◈Cross-sell CAC is near-zero — selling line #4 to an existing customer costs a fraction of a new acquisition
◈ The CEO thesis in one line: "We don't win the household by having the cheapest single service — we win it by being the only one that can put wireless, fibre, TV, security, and a parent's medical pendant on one bill. Every line we add compounds the 0.91% churn advantage. My growth plan is depth-per-household, not just subscriber count."
◈ Subscriber-interchange stickiness is modelled directionally from public churn data and TELUS's disclosed bundle mechanics (security requiring internet in the West, Mobility cross-discounts). Exact per-line churn deltas aren't publicly disclosed — the structural relationship (more services → lower churn) is well-established; precise percentages are illustrative.

The affordability critique (know the attack)

  • ✗Canada 10th most expensive globally — 26× France per GB
  • ✗Big Three own 90% — critics call it an oligopoly
  • ✗Most Canadians use under 5GB but pay for 25–50GB plans
  • ✗Retention-desk discounts ($10–20/mo) reward hagglers, not loyalty

The industry defence (know the rebuttal)

  • ✓Prices down sharply — avg plan now ~$43.51 vs old $75–85
  • ✓Vast geography, 4 people/km² — high build cost per capita
  • ✓$40B+ TELUS 5G/fibre capex — someone funds the network
  • ✓Flankers + Freedom price war pushing prices lower
◈ The regulatory reality you'd inherit: as of June 12, 2026, carriers can no longer charge activation, plan-change, upgrade, or cancellation fees — a consumer-friendly rule that makes switching frictionless and raises the stakes on churn. Combined with the CRTC wholesale-access mandate letting carriers resell into each other's territory, the regulatory wind is blowing toward lower prices and easier switching. A CEO plans for margin compression, not expansion, on the mobile line.
◈ The balanced CEO answer (for the affordability question): "Canadians have historically paid among the highest prices in the world — that's real, and I won't dismiss it. But the trend is what matters: average bills have fallen sharply, the fee ban has removed switching friction, and flanker competition is intensifying. My job isn't to defend high prices — it's to earn premium pricing through a genuinely premium, reliable, full-household experience, while our flanker brands compete hard at the value end. We win on value delivered, not on locking people in."
◈ Price-per-GB figures are from Cable.co.uk (2023 data, latest comprehensive global set); the ~$43.51 average monthly plan is a 2026 market estimate and methodologies differ (stand-alone-data GB price vs blended plan cost). Plan-tier prices vary constantly by promo cycle. Verify current numbers before quoting in an interview.

Confidential · Balance-Sheet Comparison · Q2 2026 reported

TELUS carries the
lightest balance sheet
of the Big Three.

Net debt to EBITDA is the number rating agencies and the board watch. At 3.5× TELUS is still the least levered of the Big Three, with the least absolute debt. But leverage rose in 2026 and the 3.0× target moved out a year to 2028, so the lead is narrower than it was.

Debt vs EBITDA — live pressure

needle = leverage · lower is safer

Each company's 2026 EBITDA and interest bill, ticking at its reported pace. Each bar is its net debt on one shared scale, and the solid part is the EBITDA it has earned against it this year; the marker is where it lands on Dec 31. The gauges below show where each ratio sits today.

LIVEDebt vs EBITDA · 2026 year to date
Year to date = reported first-half 2026 (Q1 + Q2) plus each company's Q2 daily pace since July 1, until Q3 is reported. EBITDA is adjusted EBITDA. Interest is what each reports: TELUS "financing costs", BCE "interest expense", Rogers "finance costs", so definitions differ slightly. Leverage is as reported at June 30, 2026. Net debt: TELUS $25.9B reported at March 31, 2026; Bell and Rogers derived as reported leverage × trailing adjusted EBITDA (Rogers states $9.99B pro forma).

Ratios aren't calculated identically across carriers — direction and ranking are robust, exact decimals approximate.

05

What this means for the chair

the interview line
◈ Say this: "On the balance sheet, TELUS still leads the Big Three — 3.5× versus Bell at 3.7× and Rogers at 3.8×, and Bell carries about $40 billion in net debt. In July 2026 we made the disciplined call to reset the dividend 55% and lower the payout ratio to 45–60% of free cash flow — the same medicine Bell took a year earlier — which frees about $2.7 billion for debt reduction through 2028 and gets us to 3.0× by the end of 2028, two years ahead of Bell. My job is to protect that lead: fund every growth move from divestiture proceeds and free cash flow, never new leverage."
◈ The one caveat to acknowledge: ratios aren't perfectly comparable — each defines "net debt" and "adjusted EBITDA" differently (Rogers adjusts 50% of subordinated notes; MLSE/Shaw distort trailing EBITDA). Quote the direction and ranking with confidence; footnote the exact decimals.
Confidential · CEO Thesis · The 100-Day Plan

Don't out-spend them.
Out-retain, out-bundle,
out-diversify them.

TELUS is deleveraging — 3.4× net debt/EBITDA today, targeting 3.0× by 2027. The winning M&A move isn't a spree. It's balance-sheet-neutral tuck-ins funded by divestitures already in motion, aimed at the metrics where Rogers and Bell are soft.

01

The constraint you inherit

read before pitching any deal

A candidate who walks in with a billion-dollar shopping list fails the room. The board's priority is deleveraging. Credibility comes from acquiring surgically, funded by the monetisation levers already public.

02

Brand loyalty — who holds customers longest

from churn → tenure

Loyalty is the inverse of churn. Average customer tenure = 1 ÷ monthly churn rate. This is TELUS's single greatest structural advantage.

◈ Tenure is derived from reported/estimated monthly postpaid churn. TELUS's 0.91% implies ~110 months of average customer life — roughly 64% longer than Rogers at ~1.5%. Loyalty scores are indexed to that relationship.

03

Where the wires end

satellite, and who gets paid where there's no fibre or copper

TELUS fibre now reaches 3.8M homes and businesses in BC, Alberta and Eastern Québec. Past the last fibre and copper line, about 400,000 Canadian households still can't buy 50/10 internet, including 1 in 8 rural homes. Starlink has become a major Canadian ISP in that gap, with 500,000+ subscribers (about one for every six TELUS internet customers), and none of what they pay goes to a Canadian carrier. TELUS can take a share without building anything. Next to $7.4B of EBITDA the share is small. The capex it avoids and the customers it keeps are what matter.

Bars: up-front capital to reach the same homes, on a scale up to 200,000 homes. Fibre at $13,530 a home counts public money alone; the satellite share needs none.
◈ The catch. Starlink is American, and Ottawa is moving away from it: "Starlink, we will diversify away from, no question," Prime Minister Carney said on Sep 24, 2026. Ontario cancelled its $100M Starlink contract for 15,000 rural homes in March 2025. The Canadian alternative, Telesat Lightspeed, now starts service at the end of Q1 2028, and Ottawa has secured up to $600M of its capacity. Canadian pension money is behind SpaceX too: Ontario Teachers' stake is worth about US$8.7B. Waiting also costs: in New Zealand, Starlink became the largest rural ISP (27% share against Spark's 23%), mostly from customers leaving copper. So sign short, sell it as TELUS Satellite, keep the customer and the bill, and be ready to move homes to Telesat in 2028.
◈ The CEO line: "Where our fibre ends, we won't spend $13,500 a home to reach a few thousand homes. We'll sell satellite under the TELUS name, keep the customer and the bundle, and keep the capital for fibre that pays back. Phones get AST, which we part-own. Homes get the best constellation on a short contract: Starlink today, Telesat when it's ready."
◈ How these numbers are built. 50/10 access: 97.4% of households nationally, 87.4% rural (ISED, 2024 data, updated May 2026); ≈400,000 households is 2.6% of ~15.5M (Statistics Canada). BC 97% (ISED/BC) and Alberta 98.1% (Sep 2026) applied to 2021 Census households give ~90,000 in TELUS's home provinces. TELUS fibre: ~3.8M homes and businesses (Q2 2026 MD&A). Starlink in Canada: 500,000+ subscribers (Jul 2025); 2026 prices from Starlink's Canadian price list; ~$95 blended is our estimate. SpaceX gateways and D2C use: SpaceX submission to ISED, Aug 2026. Rogers Satellite $15 (Jul 2025); Bell free on top two plans or ~$10–15 (Oct 2025); TELUS–AST agreement and equity stake (Mar 2026). The model: EBITDA is 80% of TELUS's revenue; phones at $10 a month with TELUS keeping half; leverage uses $25.9B of net debt at 3.5× (≈$7.4B EBITDA); the phone line kept uses Q2 2026 ARPU of $56.36. Telesat service date: Telesat, Mar 2026. New Zealand shares: Commerce Commission, reported Jun 2026.

From the air
to the

How a telecom network actually works — the physical path a packet takes, the latency budget it must fit inside, the protocol stack it climbs, the spectrum physics that governs everything, and exactly who holds which megahertz in Canada.

01

Wireless vs wireline — the two halves

every telco runs both businesses

A telecom company is really two companies sharing a brand. Wireless sells mobility — air, towers, spectrum, a subscriber who can churn next month. Wireline sells a physical drop into a building — fibre in the ground, a 20-year asset, a household that almost never leaves. They have opposite economics, and TELUS wins differently in each.

📡 WIRELESS
Mobility · spectrum · towers
AssetSpectrum licences
DeliveryRadio waves, shared air

Churn0.91% monthly — mobile

SHARED

Same billing + bundle
Fibre backhauls the towers
Bundle = lower churn on both
↓
This is the convergence play: wireline fibre is what carries wireless traffic back from the tower. Owning both means you don't rent from a rival.
🔌 WIRELINE
Fibre · copper · coax
AssetFibre in the ground
DeliveryLight in glass, dedicated

TELUS brandTELUS PureFibre
◈ The asymmetry that drives strategy: wireless ARPU is falling (−2.8%) while internet ARPU is rising (+6%). Wireless is a rented relationship; wireline is an owned one. A fibre drop is a 20–30 year asset with a near-permanent customer attached, and the same fibre also backhauls the cell towers above it. That's why TELUS has committed $45B+ to PureFibre — it's simultaneously the wireline product, the wireless backbone, and the churn moat.
02

PureFibre vs Bell Fibe — the fibre war

same technology · different geography

The most important wireline matchup in Canada. Here's the honest read: both run the same underlying technology — XGS-PON, 100% fibre to the home, symmetrical speeds. Neither has a physics advantage. The war is won on footprint, execution, price certainty and who got there first. Hover a row.

Where TELUS wins

  • ✓The West is owned — BC and Alberta are PureFibre country, last-mile owned outright
  • ✓5-year price lock — Bell guarantees only 2 years. The single clearest differentiator.
  • ✓Copper retirement — actively migrating customers to fibre free, so the base is all-fibre
  • ✓100% FTTH purity — no hybrid coax anywhere in the footprint

Where Bell wins

  • ✓Scale — ~7.3M premises passed, Canada's largest FTTH network
  • ✓Top speed — 8 Gbps tiers in select ON/QC; TELUS tops out ~3 Gbps
  • ✓Ontario + Quebec density — the two biggest markets are home turf
  • ✓Ziply acquisition — buying further fibre scale (~$5B)
◈ The regulatory twist that shaped this: a 2023 CRTC decision requiring Bell to open its Ontario/Quebec fibre to wholesale competitors prompted Bell to scale back its planned fibre build and cut its 2025 target, arguing the ruling discouraged investment. That same wholesale regime is how TELUS is now entering Ontario and Quebec — competing on Bell's turf partly over Bell's own fibre. Worth knowing: expansion via wholesale carries thinner margins than owned last-mile, which is a real question a board will ask.
◈ The CEO line: "Bell has more homes passed and a faster headline tier. I'm not going to out-trench them in Ontario. What I own is the West outright, a 100% fibre base with no coax legacy, and the only five-year price lock in the market. We win the fibre war on certainty and retention, not on a speed-test number almost no household actually uses."
03

The signal chain — click any stage

phone → RU → DU → CU → core → internet

Every call, stream and text follows this path in milliseconds. Packets flow outbound in amber, return in teal. Click a node to open its full technical spec below — hardware, protocol, latency budget and what breaks if it fails.

04

The latency budget

where the milliseconds go

5G promises single-digit millisecond response. That budget gets spent across every hop — and it's why the CU and edge compute moved closer to the tower. Watch the waterfall fill.

◈ Indicative budget for a 5G Standalone URLLC-class path. Real-world consumer latency is higher (typically 20–40 ms round trip to a public server) because of internet transit beyond the core. 3GPP targets 1 ms on the air interface alone; the end-to-end figure depends on how far the application server sits — which is exactly why edge compute at the CU/midhaul layer is the architectural answer.
05

The protocol stack

what wraps your data at each layer

Your data gets wrapped in envelopes on the way down and unwrapped on the way up. Hover a layer to see what it does and where it runs.

◈ Since 4G the network core is all-IP — control plane tunnelled over SCTP/IP, user plane over GTP/UDP/IP. Before that, cellular internals were circuit-switched, a legacy of the network's origins as a voice system. That single change is what turned carriers from telephone companies into data companies.
06

RAN topology — the three architectures

click to morph the network

The tower used to hold everything. Modern networks split it apart and centralise the brains — cheaper to densify, and the reason 5G can slice itself into private networks. Click an architecture to watch the topology rearrange.

07

Spectrum physics — why frequency is destiny

live wave propagation

One physical trade-off governs the entire industry: low frequency travels far but carries little; high frequency carries enormous data but barely travels. The waves below are drawn to their real relative wavelength — watch how the low band stretches across the map while mmWave crowds into a few hundred metres.

◈ Wavelength λ = c/f. At 600 MHz λ is half a metre — it diffracts around hills and penetrates walls. At 26 GHz λ is ~11 mm — it behaves almost like light, blocked by a hand or a pane of glass. This is why carriers need all three bands, and why the 3500/3800 MHz mid-band — reach and capacity both acceptable — was the most contested spectrum in Canadian history.
08

Who holds what — Canadian spectrum

MHz by carrier · ISED licences

Spectrum is licensed by ISED through auctions, then held as time-limited licences per geographic tier. Bars are scaled to total holdings — hover for the band split.

◈ The contiguity story: TELUS's 3500 MHz sits adjacent to its 3800 MHz, forming ~100 MHz of contiguous mid-band across ~96% of Canada — deployable with a single radio, where Bell and Rogers must run carrier aggregation across separated blocks. Contiguity is a genuine cost and latency advantage that never shows up in a simple MHz count. Flankers and prepaid brands own no spectrum — they ride the parent's licences. Figures from the ISED 3800 MHz auction (Nov 2023) and 3500 MHz holdings (2024); set-aside blocks reserved for regional players shaped the outcome. Verify against ISED's published tables before quoting.
09

1G to 5G — what actually changed

forty years, and the one shift that mattered
◈ Each generation roughly a decade apart. The jump that mattered commercially wasn't speed — it was 4G moving the network onto IP. 5G Standalone repeats that shift by making the core cloud-native and sliceable: one physical network, many logical networks, each with its own guaranteed latency and bandwidth.
10

How the money actually works

where a dollar of ARPU goes

Telecom is a capital machine: buy spectrum, build network, rent it monthly, repeat. Enormous fixed costs, near-zero marginal cost per extra gigabyte.

The cost stack

  • 1Spectrum licences — billions upfront at auction. A sunk 20-year bet.
  • 2Network capex — towers, fibre, radios. TELUS ~$2.3B/yr, trending down as the 5G build matures.
  • 3Subscriber acquisition — device subsidies, commissions, marketing. The biggest variable cost.
  • 4Operating — backhaul leases, power, site rent, staff, roaming settlements.

Why churn is the whole game

  • ◈Network cost is fixed — same whether 9M or 11M people use it
  • ◈Every retained subscriber is nearly pure margin on an already-built network
  • ◈Every churned one must be re-bought at full acquisition cost
  • ◈That's why 0.91% churn compounds into the strongest economics of the Big Three
◈ The industry in one sentence: you spend billions on spectrum and steel to build a pipe that costs almost nothing to run, then you win or lose on how long people stay attached to it.

03

The three commitments

what I'd say publicly on day one

A new CEO gets one credibility budget. I'd spend it on three promises that are specific, measurable, and survivable.

Commit

Churn stays under 1%

The 0.91% is the franchise. It ticked to ~1.11% in Q3 under promo pressure — I own that number publicly and report it every quarter. Bundle depth, not discounting, is how we hold it.

Commit

3.0× leverage by 2027

No new leverage for any growth move. Every acquisition is tuck-in scale or funded by divestitures already in motion. The board's #1 KPI becomes mine.

Commit

Fibre + health, not scale

We stop trying to out-scale Rogers. Capital goes to PureFibre depth and the health/digital flywheel — the two assets rivals cannot buy back.

04

What I won't do in 100 days

restraint is a strategy

Half of a first-100-days plan is the discipline to not act. These are deliberate holds — each one a mistake a new CEO is tempted into.

Deliberate holds

  • ✗No reorg. Restructuring before you understand the org destroys more value than it creates. Not before day 120.
  • ✗No big acquisition. Leverage discipline is the promise. Nothing that breaks it, however good the asset looks.
  • ✗No price war. Matching Quebecor's $34 plans on the flagship torches ARPU. That fight belongs to Koodo and Public.
  • ✗No new strategy deck. The strategy is sound. Execution and sequencing are the gap, not vision.

The hard question I'd expect

"Churn hit 1.11% and mobile net adds fell to 207K. Is the moat eroding?"

Honest answer: the mobile moat is under real pressure — that's promo intensity plus the June 2026 fee ban making switching frictionless. But churn is a household metric, not a handset one. A mobile-only customer leaves easily; a household with fibre, security and a parent's medical pendant does not. My response isn't to defend the mobile number in isolation — it's to raise services-per-household so the number stops being fragile. That's measurable, and I'd report it.

Three ways to take a square

the Q4 playbook
01

Winback

25K · squares we used to own

Former TELUS and Koodo subscribers from the last 24 months. They know the network, need no education, and convert far above cold prospects. Segment by why they left, not just when.

  • →Lead with the 5-year price lock — it answers the grievance that caused most exits
  • →Device-balance buyout for anyone still financed elsewhere
  • →Hold back service-quality churners until the local fix is confirmed
02

40K · squares changing hands

The regulator now forces our rivals to tell their own customers when to shop. Under Policy 2026-67 they must flag an expiring promo and hand over alternatives. Be standing there when it happens.

  • →Build the competitor promo-expiry calendar; concentrate spend on those weeks
  • →Own paid search on port-out and switching intent
  • →Advertise the 4-hour port as a promise, not fine print

Flank

25K · squares priced out of reach

Never fight Videotron's $34 pricing with the flagship — that torches ARPU across the whole base. Koodo and Public take the value war.

  • →Public Mobile is the only discount brand with true 5G
  • →Koodo goes straight at the Fido and Virgin switcher
  • →Flagship pricing never moves
03

Plan pricing, 2020 → today

flagship vs flanker vs discount

Six years of Canadian wireless pricing in one chart. The government set a 25% reduction target off a 2020 benchmark; ISED confirmed it was hit by Q1 2022. Then the floor kept falling as flanker and discount brands went to war — and since late 2025 prices have been climbing back. In April 2026 Fido, Koodo and Virgin Plus all raised prices in near-lockstep.

◈ Source: ISED Price Comparisons of Wireline, Wireless and Internet Services, 17th edition (2024 data, published 2025), plus carrier pricing observed through 2026. ISED's tracked tiers differ slightly year to year as carriers discontinue and relaunch plans — 2025 and 2026 points are observed market pricing, not ISED-published figures, and should be treated as directional. The Big Three discontinued several tracked tiers entirely (Rogers 2023, Bell and TELUS 2024), which is itself part of the story: when a price gets uncomfortable, the plan disappears rather than drops.
04

In-market vs BTL

the two price books

Every carrier runs two price books. In-market is what you see advertised — the acquisition offer, public, competitive, measurable. BTL (below-the-line) is what the retention desk hands out when you threaten to leave: discretionary credits, typically $20–$60/month for 6–24 months, never advertised, never in the price list. The gap between them is where margin quietly leaks.

IN-MARKET
Above the line · public
Who sees itEveryone — advertised
PurposeAcquisition, port-ins
Typical 2026$45–$65 · 50–125GB
Governed byPublished price list
MarginModelled, predictable
MeasurableYes — full attribution
Brand effectBuilds the price promise
THE GAP
$20–60
per month, per saved customer
↕
A loyal customer pays the in-market rate. A customer who threatens to leave gets the BTL rate. The gap is the reward we pay for disloyalty — and under Policy 2026-67 we now have to tell customers when their promo ends, which means everyone learns to ask.
BTL
Below the line · retention desk
Who sees itOnly those who threaten
PurposeSave a churning line
Typical credit$20–60/mo, 6–24 months
Governed byAgent discretion
MarginEroded, unbudgeted
MeasurablePoorly — no attribution
Brand effectTeaches customers to haggle

Why BTL is structurally broken

  • ✗It rewards the wrong behaviour. The quiet, loyal customer subsidises the one who calls to cancel every year.
  • ✗It is invisible in the P&L. Spread across thousands of agent decisions, it never appears as a marketing line — it appears as ARPU decay.
  • ✗2026-67 blew it open. Carriers must now notify customers before a promo expires and show alternatives. The haggling cohort just became everyone.
  • ✗Zero switching cost. With fees banned and 4-hour porting, the threat behind every BTL call is now completely credible.

The TELUS answer — collapse the gap

  • ✓The 5-year price lock is the anti-BTL product. If the price never moves, there is nothing to call and renegotiate.
  • ✓Move spend above the line. A dollar in an advertised offer acquires; a dollar at the retention desk only defends — and teaches the customer to come back for more.
  • ✓Cap agent discretion, fund the base. Narrow BTL authority; redirect the budget into in-market offers and bundle attach.
  • ✓Measure it. BTL credit as a % of ARPU becomes a reported internal metric, not an invisible leak.
◈ The CEO line: "We run two price books and only one of them is honest. The retention desk quietly hands out twenty to sixty dollars a month to whoever threatens to leave, while the customer who never complains pays full freight. That is not a pricing strategy, it is a tax on loyalty — and now that the regulator makes us tell every customer when their promo expires, the whole base is about to learn the trick. My answer is the five-year price lock: one price, published, held. Collapse the gap before the market collapses it for us."
◈ BTL credit ranges ($20–60/month, 6–24 months) reflect widely reported retention-desk practice across Canadian carriers, not a TELUS-disclosed figure. Carriers do not publish BTL economics. Treat as directional market context.

Governance, gates & risk

who owns it, what stops it

Named owner per workstream, three hard gates before anything ships, and the risks I'd want on record rather than discovered mid-quarter.

Winback — data, segmentation, offerVP Customer Retention, ON+QC
In-Market — media, search, promo calendarVP Acquisition Marketing

GATE 1
Legal & privacy

Lapsed-base file clears General Counsel on data source, retention period, contact method — before any customer is contacted. No soft launch ahead of clearance.

GATE 2
Regulatory

Porting-related messaging — the 4-hour promise, any switching-friction comparison — reviewed against CRTC conduct rules before it reaches paid media.

GATE 3
Financial

Each channel reviewed at day-30 and day-60 against its CAC ceiling. No credible path to 3:1 by day 60 → paused, not carried on hope.

07

The quarter, week by week

Oct → Dec

Q4 has a shape. Load the machine in October, spend hard through Black Friday and the holiday upgrade window, then convert volume into depth before the quarter closes.

The target — and the honest math

  • ◈90K gross adds across ON+QC in the quarter
  • ◈75K net after churn — roughly 0.32 share points
  • ◈Split: 25K winback · 40K in-market · 25K flanker
  • ⚠Reality check: TELUS added 207K mobile subs nationally across all of 2025. 75K net in two provinces in one quarter is aggressive but real — I'd rather commit to a number we hit than promise a share point we miss.

Guardrails

  • ✗No flagship price cuts. Volume bought with ARPU isn't growth.
  • ✗No unfunded subsidies. Every one carries a payback test against the lock term.
  • ✗Kill anything under 3:1 LTV:CAC. At $57 ARPU and ~110-month life the Q4 model runs 12.5:1 blended; at 1.5% churn it still clears 7.6:1.
  • ✗No winback contact until legal clears source, timing and method.
◈ Compliance checkpoint. CRTC winback restrictions were set for wireline ILEC/CLEC porting (Decision 2006-28) and were not extended to wireless in the same form — but porting conduct is regulated, and the June 2026 rules explicitly ban porting delays as a retention tactic. Every winback campaign clears regulatory review before launch.
◈ The rally line: "Twenty-three million subscribers, and we hold one in five. Q4 is the only quarter where every square is in play at once. We don't buy the board with flagship discounts — we take it at the moment customers are already shopping, because the regulator now makes our competitors tell them when that is. Winback who knows us. Go In-Market for who's leaving. Let Koodo and Public hold the value line. Seventy-five thousand net, reported publicly. Go TELUS Go."

Listing & distribution

the shareholder facts

Where it trades

  • ◈TSX: T (Toronto) · NYSE: TU (New York)
  • ◈Market cap ~$21.5B, share ~$13.50
  • ◈P/E ~18.5 · EPS ~$0.73
  • ◈Fiscal year ends Dec 31

The dividend reset

  • ↘Quarterly cut to $0.1875 (−55%), effective Oct 1 2026
  • ◈2026 annual ~$1.21; 2027 run-rate ~$0.75
  • ◈Payout target lowered to 45–60% of trailing FCF
  • ◈Dividend growth model withdrawn; DRIP discount paused

Why the reset

  • ◈Prior yield had ballooned to ~11% — unsustainable at 100%+ payout
  • ◈Frees cash to hit 3.0× leverage by 2027
  • ◈Mirrors Bell's 2025 reset — sector-wide discipline
  • ◈DRIP + share-purchase plan still available, fee-free
◈ The IR narrative: "The reset isn't weakness — it's the same disciplined capital allocation that gets us to 3.0× ahead of both rivals. A lower, well-covered dividend plus record free cash flow is a stronger equity story than an 11% yield the market didn't believe."
